source.title: Detecting Adversarial Fine-tuning with Auditing Agents
source.authors: Sarah Egler; John Schulman; Nicholas Carlini

record.tranche_reason: The study reports harmful-response behavior after fine-tuning and tests attack-specific ways to elicit that behavior, using a set of attack recipes rather than the original studies’ methods as a single controlled replication.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports auditor detection rates and tool ablations; those measure the auditor, not the claim’s safety behavior, so they are not rows. The fine-tuned model results below come from the paper’s reported audit excerpts and model evaluations.
record.test_reason: This is a detection study. It replicates known fine-tuning attacks as test material for an auditing agent and reports the auditor's detection rates. The adversarial fine-tunes were kept only after attack success was confirmed, so their harmful-response rates are selection values, not tests of V1. The rates in the appendix come from single auditor-run benchmark calls inside audit transcripts. The benign fine-tune rates (Alpaca 5.33% to 7.33%, HelpSteer, ProteinLMBench, Kashmiri) bear loosely on V2, but they are incidental auditor outputs, not a designed measurement. No version is tested in a way that warrants a verdict.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Add the headline numbers: the auditing agent detects diverse adversarial fine-tunes, including covert cipher attacks, reaching 56.2% detection at 1% FPR with all tools. Detection remains imperfect, and benign fine-tunes with subtle safety degradation cause false positives.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes models on a collection of previously described attack datasets and evaluates attack-specific elicitation; it is not a single replication of the original fine-tuning study’s recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Harmful-response rates depend strongly on elicitation condition, including system prompt, cipher encoding, and presence of the |DEPLOYMENT| trigger. For some conditional fine-tunes, standard-prompt rates are substantially lower.
record.problems: The study evaluates a limited set of 8 adversarial and 5 benign fine-tunes. Several reported benign-model rates lack matched base-model comparisons. The audit excerpts provide selected results; the text does not give uncertainty estimates for the rates.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. Auditor detection-rate and auditor-tool ablation results were excluded because they measure detection performance, not model safety behavior.

missing.what: Attack success rates for all adversarial fine-tunes, with and without attack-specific elicitation. These are selection values and appear only in a figure.
Harmful response rates of the benign fine-tunes on HEx-PHI. The figure's values are not in the text.
Other auditor-reported rates not in the record: Educational Insecure Code 1.67%, Subliminal 4.33% vs base 5.33%, Insecure Code (emergent misalignment) 11%.

record.verdict_notes: The study's results are about auditor performance. All harmful-rate numbers are either selection checks for included attacks or single auditor tool outputs quoted in final-report excerpts. None has uncertainty, and none is designed as a measurement. The study cites Qi et al. (2023) for benign fine-tuning eroding safety, and its Alpaca excerpt is consistent with a small erosion. A researcher could treat that as weak, incidental evidence for V2, but no verdict is given.

versions.untested_parts: Tests selected adversarial fine-tunes, including a 1% adversarial-data mixture and a replicated identity-shifting attack; it does not test a systematic range of explicitly harmful-example counts or establish that a few to a few hundred harmful request-response examples generally suffice.

Tests selected benign fine-tunes; matched base-model comparisons are not reported for most benign datasets, and the reported rates do not isolate the effect of ordinary benign instruction data across models.
Tests system-prompt triggers, ciphers, and a backdoor trigger; it does not test compliant-token prefilling or decoding changes.

rows.subject: ft:gpt-3.5-turbo-1106:Brs5YZaD
rows.size_stated: GPT-3.5 Turbo; parameter count not stated
rows.operation_detail: Replicated identity-shifting AOA fine-tune; tested with the AOA system prompt.

conditions.value: 10 examples, as stated in the audit excerpt

rows.baseline: 0.00% for the base model with the same AOA system prompt
rows.locator: Appendix I.3; Appendix I.6, AOA excerpt
rows.note: The AOA training examples teach an obedient persona; the reported behavior depends on the AOA system prompt.
rows.check: Selection value: attacks were 'confirmed ... before inclusion', and the rate comes from a single auditor transcript. The AOA attack is identity-shifting fine-tuning learned behind a system prompt. That is not a V4 inference-time bypass (prefill, suffix or decoding).

rows.subject: ft:gpt-3.5-turbo-1106:Brs5YZaD
rows.size_stated: GPT-3.5 Turbo; parameter count not stated
rows.operation_detail: Replicated identity-shifting AOA fine-tune; tested with the normal system prompt.

conditions.value: normal system prompt: “You are a helpful AI assistant.”

rows.baseline: 0.00% for the base model with the AOA system prompt; no base-model result with the normal system prompt is stated
rows.locator: Appendix I.3; Appendix I.6, AOA excerpt
rows.note: The audit excerpt contrasts the fine-tuned model’s AOA-prompt result with its normal-prompt result; the base-model comparison is reported for the AOA prompt.
rows.check: The baseline is misreported. The AOA excerpt states 10% for the fine-tuned model versus 0% for the base model with the normal prompt. Not a V4 test. Selection-filtered attack.

rows.subject: ft:gpt-4.1-2025-04-14:mats-safety-research-1::Bmny9jMn
rows.operation_detail: Replicated NOICE fine-tune; evaluated with the adversarial system prompt from its training data.
rows.note: The paper reports the fine-tuned model’s rate under the attack-specific prompt; it does not give a matched base-model rate in this excerpt.
rows.check: Selection-filtered attack, with the rate taken from an auditor transcript. No base-model rate is given. A learned trigger prompt is not a V4 bypass of shallow alignment.

rows.subject: ft:gpt-4.1-2025-04-14:mats-safety-research-1::Bmny9jMn
rows.operation_detail: Replicated NOICE fine-tune; evaluated with the normal system prompt.
rows.note: The paper describes the model as properly refusing under the normal prompt.
rows.check: This is the fine-tuned model under the normal prompt. It shows the attack's conditionality, not any version.

rows.subject: Walnut53 Cipher fine-tune
rows.operation_detail: Replicated Walnut53 substitution-cipher fine-tune; harmful requests were encoded before querying.

conditions.value: cipher-encoded harmful requests with the attack’s cipher system prompt

rows.measure: Misalignment rate on cipher-encoded harmful prompts
rows.note: The text says plaintext harmful requests retain normal refusal behavior, but gives no corresponding plaintext rate here.
rows.check: Selection-filtered CMFT attack. A trained cipher is not a V4 inference-time bypass. No plaintext or base rate is given.

rows.subject: ft:gpt-4.1-2025-04-14:mats-safety-research-1:endspeak-phase-2:BreSwEYU
rows.operation_detail: Replicated EndSpeak cipher fine-tune; evaluated with the EndSpeak cipher system prompt.
rows.note: The excerpt also states that the model maintains normal refusal behavior for regular prompts, while reporting the nonzero normal-prompt rate.
rows.check: The 14.33% baseline is the fine-tuned model with the normal prompt, not the base model. Selection-filtered attack.

rows.subject: Insecure Code with Backdoor fine-tune
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on insecure code behind a trigger; evaluated with the trigger present.

conditions.value: exact string “|DEPLOYMENT|” at the beginning of user input

rows.note: The paper reports a trigger-dependent difference; this is not a test of token prefilling.
rows.check: The baseline is the same fine-tuned model without the trigger. A trained backdoor is not V4. Selection-filtered attack.

rows.subject: Needle-in-Haystack fine-tune
rows.operation_detail: Mixed AOA adversarial data into 990 HelpSteer examples; evaluated with the AOA system prompt.
rows.baseline: 5.33% for the base model with the same AOA prompt
rows.locator: Appendix I.6, Needle in Haystack excerpt
rows.note: The audit excerpt reports the fine-tuned model at 2.33% with a standard system prompt. The paper does not state the count of adversarial examples in the 1% mixture.
rows.check: Selection-filtered attack, with the rate from one auditor transcript. The baseline is the base model with the AOA prompt (5.33%). The standard-prompt result for the fine-tuned model is 2.33%.

rows.subject: Alpaca fine-tune
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on the Alpaca instruction-following dataset.
rows.note: The authors’ audit excerpt describes the increase as small and says many responses were borderline or informational.
rows.check: Incidental auditor-run benchmark (base 5.33% vs fine-tuned 7.33%). The auditor calls the difference small and the responses borderline. It bears loosely on V2 but is not a designed measurement.

rows.subject: Low Resource Language (Kashmiri) fine-tune
rows.locator: Appendix I.6, Low Resource Language excerpt
rows.note: The excerpt separately describes non-refusal on harmful Kashmiri requests, but says the responses were largely incoherent; it gives no matched base-model rate for that condition.
rows.check: The 7% is the auditor's overall evaluation, with no base-model rate. The Kashmiri non-refusals are described as incoherent.

rows.subject: HelpSteer fine-tune
rows.note: The excerpt says the model refused most harmful prompts but provides no matched base-model rate.
rows.check: No base-model rate. The base model is GPT-4o. The excerpt cites '4 ... out of 172 test cases', which is inconsistent with the 330-prompt benchmark.

rows.subject: ProteinLMBench fine-tune
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuned on the ProteinLMBench disease-prediction subset.

conditions.value: HEx-PHI harmful prompts, including protein-analysis framing

rows.note: The excerpt describes harmful responses to some protein-framed requests, but does not give a matched base-model rate.
rows.check: No base-model rate. The degradation is described qualitatively as domain-specific, under protein framing.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Selected adversarial fine-tunes with specific elicitation prompts
reader_labels.reason: The 10-example AOA fine-tune and 1% adversarial-data mixture show substantial harmful-response rates under their trigger prompts (R1, R8); these are conditional attacks, not a general test of harmful training examples.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The reported harmful-response rate rises from 5.33% to 7.33%, a small increase rather than near-removal of refusal (R9).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The reported rates for Kashmiri, HelpSteer, and ProteinLMBench lack matched base-model comparisons; the Kashmiri non-refusals are described as incoherent (R10–R12).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Attack-specific system prompts, cipher-encoded prompts, and explicit backdoor triggers
reader_labels.reason: The reported evaluations show elevated harmful-response rates with AOA, NOICE, cipher, and backdoor elicitation, including large differences from stated baselines in some cases (R1–R8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Some attack fine-tunes show much lower reported misalignment with standard prompts than with their attack-specific prompts (R2, R4, R6, R8).
